key_terms.meaning: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, so Z = R, the current is maximum and in phase with V; f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC))
At series resonance V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>C</sub> = QV
Susceptances cancel; the tank impedance is maximum and the supply current minimum
f₀ = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − (r/L)²); dynamic resistance R<sub>D</sub> = L/(rC)
Q = 2π × W<sub>max</sub>/W<sub>lost</sub>; series Q = ω₀L/R = (1/R)√(L/C); parallel Q = R/(ω₀L)
BW = f₂ − f₁ = f₀/Q; for series RLC, BW = R/(2πL)
f₁f₂ = f₀²; exact ω₁,₂ = ω₀(√(1 + 1/(4Q²)) ∓ 1/(2Q)); about f₀ ± BW/2 for Q ≥ 10
f₀/BW = Q; the higher Q, the sharper the separation of nearby frequencies
f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πRC), where a first-order RC gain is 0.707 (−3 dB) and the phase is ∓45°
|H| = 1/√(1 + Q²(ω/ω₀ − ω₀/ω)²) for the resistor voltage of a series RLC
Semicircle of diameter V/(fixed element); full circle of diameter V/R for series RLC with ω varied
L = NΦ/i in henry; |e| = L|di/dt|
M = N₂Φ₂₁/i₁ in henry; |e₂| = M|di₁/dt|
k = M/√(L₁L₂), 0 ≤ k ≤ 1
Currents entering both dots give aiding flux and +M terms; one entering and one leaving give −M
L<sub>eq</sub> = L₁ + L₂ ± 2M (aiding +, opposing −)
n = N₂/N₁; V₂/V₁ = n; I₂/I₁ = 1/n; Z<sub>in</sub> = Z<sub>L</sub>/n²
Z<sub>in</sub> = jωL₁ + (ωM)²/(jωL₂ + Z<sub>L</sub>) for a linear transformer
Φ = F/R<sub>total</sub> with F = NI and R = l/(μ₀μ<sub>r</sub> A); series reluctances add
L = N²/R<sub>total</sub>

takeaways: Series resonance: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)); the impedance drops to R, the current peaks and V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>C</sub> = QV.
Parallel resonance is the dual: susceptances cancel, the tank impedance peaks and the supply current dips; a real coil lowers f₀ and gives R<sub>D</sub> = L/(rC).
One number, Q, sets bandwidth (BW = f₀/Q) and selectivity; the half-power frequencies satisfy f₁f₂ = f₀².
An RC section gives one −3 dB corner at f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πRC) and a 20 dB per decade slope; a series RLC gives a band-pass peak whose width is f₀/Q.
Vary one element and the current phasor of a series RL or RC circuit runs on a semicircle of diameter V over the fixed element; parallel resonance happens where the shifted circle cuts the V axis.
Self-inductance is a coil reacting to its own current; mutual inductance is the shared flux reaching a second coil, with M = k√(L₁L₂) and k ≤ 1.
The dot convention fixes the sign of every mutual term: aiding gives L₁ + L₂ + 2M, opposing L₁ + L₂ − 2M.
An ideal transformer scales voltage by n, current by 1/n and impedance by n²; a linear transformer adds the reflected impedance (ωM)²/(jωL₂ + Z<sub>L</sub>).
Magnetic circuits follow Ohm's law in magnetic form: Φ = NI/R<sub>total</sub>, and a 1 mm air gap can take more MMF than 0.4 m of iron.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for the impedance expression first, then the resonance condition, then Q and bandwidth pushed through a numerical part. Coupled-coil and transformer questions expect the dot-convention signs in the mesh equations and the turns-ratio relations, and most syllabi ask for a magnetic circuit with an air gap solved by reluctances.

bank.q: Define series resonance. Starting from the impedance of a series RLC circuit, derive the resonant frequency and show that the current is maximum and in phase with the voltage at resonance. Draw the phasor diagram at resonance.
outline: At resonance Z = R, the minimum |Z|
I = V/R is maximum and in phase with V
Phasor diagram: V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> equal and opposite
answer: Definition. A series RLC circuit is in resonance when its inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, XL = XC. The net reactance is then zero, the circuit is purely resistive, and the source voltage and current are in phase.

answer.text: Impedance. With one current I through R, L and C at angular frequency ω = 2πf:
answer.pre:
Z = R + jX<sub>L</sub> − jX<sub>C</sub> = R + j(ωL − 1/(ωC))
|Z| = √(R² + (ωL − 1/(ωC))²)
φ = arctan[(ωL − 1/(ωC))/R]

answer.text: Resonant frequency. Set the imaginary part to zero:
answer.pre:
ω₀L = 1/(ω₀C)
ω₀² = 1/(LC)
ω₀ = 1/√(LC) rad/s,   f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) Hz

answer: Maximum current. R does not depend on frequency and (ωL − 1/(ωC))² ≥ 0, so |Z| ≥ R, with equality only at ω₀. For a fixed source voltage V, I = V/|Z| is therefore largest at ω₀, where I₀ = V/R. Below ω₀ the capacitor dominates and the current leads; above ω₀ the inductor dominates and the current lags.
Phase. At ω₀ the angle φ = arctan(0/R) = 0, so I is in phase with V and the power factor is 1.

answer.text: Phasor diagram at resonance. Take I as reference. VR = IR lies along I; VL = IXL leads I by 90°; VC = IXC lags I by 90°. Because XL = XC, VL and VC are equal and opposite and cancel, so V = VR.

answer: Check with numbers. R = 10 Ω, L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF, V = 10 V: ω₀ = 1/√(10⁻⁸) = 10 000 rad/s, f₀ = 1591.5 Hz; XL = XC = 100 Ω; I₀ = 10/10 = 1 A in phase with V; VL = VC = 100 V, ten times the source, and they cancel.

bank.q: Explain parallel resonance for an ideal RLC tank and for a practical tank (a coil of resistance r and inductance L in parallel with C). Derive the resonant frequency and the dynamic resistance of the practical tank, and state the effect of a resistance in the capacitor branch.
outline: Ideal tank: Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)); ω₀ = 1/√(LC); Z = R maximum
Practical tank: coil admittance (r − jωL)/(r² + ω²L²)

answer.text: Ideal tank. R, L and C in parallel share the voltage V, so their admittances add:
answer.pre:
Y = 1/R + jωC + 1/(jωL) = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL))
Resonance: ω₀C = 1/(ω₀L)  →  ω₀ = 1/√(LC)
At ω₀: Y = 1/R (minimum), Z = R (maximum), I<sub>s</sub> = V/R (minimum)

answer: Current magnification. At ω₀ the branch currents are IL = V/(ω₀L) and IC = Vω₀C. They are equal and 180° apart, so they cancel in the supply line. Each is Q times Is, with Q = R/(ω₀L) = ω₀CR. The circuit is called a rejector or current-resonant circuit.

answer.text: Practical tank: admittance. The coil branch is r + jωL and the capacitor branch is 1/(jωC):
answer.pre:
Y<sub>coil</sub> = 1/(r + jωL) = (r − jωL)/(r² + ω²L²)
Y = r/(r² + ω²L²) + j[ωC − ωL/(r² + ω²L²)]

answer.text: Resonant frequency. Unity power factor needs the imaginary part to vanish:
answer.pre:
ω₀C = ω₀L/(r² + ω₀²L²)
r² + ω₀²L² = L/C                     (call this result A)
ω₀² = 1/(LC) − r²/L²
f₀ = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − r²/L²)

answer: The resistance pulls f₀ below the ideal value 1/(2π√(LC)). If r²/L² ≥ 1/(LC), that is r ≥ √(L/C), there is no real f₀ and the tank never reaches unity power factor.

answer.text: Dynamic resistance. At f₀ only the real part is left. Use result A:
answer.pre:
Y(ω₀) = r/(r² + ω₀²L²) = r/(L/C) = rC/L
R<sub>D</sub> = 1/Y(ω₀) = L/(rC)

answer: With the coil Q = ω₀L/r, R<sub>D</sub> = (r² + ω₀²L²)/r = r(1 + Q²), about Q²r for a good coil. A small r gives a large R<sub>D</sub> and a small supply current.

answer.text: Resistance in the capacitor branch. With RC in series with C, the same step (total susceptance zero) gives:

answer: With R<sub>C</sub> = 0 it reduces to the practical-tank result. If r = R<sub>C</sub> = √(L/C), numerator and denominator are equal for every ω: the tank is resistive at all frequencies.

answer.text: Check with numbers. r = 10 Ω, L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF, V = 10 V:

bank.q: Define the quality factor of a series RLC circuit from stored and dissipated energy and derive Q = (1/R)√(L/C). Derive the half-power frequencies and show that BW = f₀/Q and f₀ = √(f₁f₂). Explain the effect of varying Q on the resonance curve.
outline: W<sub>max</sub> = ½LI<sub>m</sub>², W<sub>lost</sub> = ½I<sub>m</sub>²R/f₀ → Q = ω₀L/R = (1/R)√(L/C)
ω₂ − ω₁ = ω₀/Q and ω₁ω₂ = ω₀²
Larger Q: narrower band, same f₀
answer: Definition. Q = 2π × (maximum energy stored)/(energy dissipated per cycle). It is dimensionless and says how many radians of oscillation the stored energy lasts.

answer.text: Series RLC at resonance. With current i = Im sin ω₀t, the energy in L and C together is constant at resonance and equals the inductor's peak energy:
answer.pre:
W<sub>max</sub>  = ½ L I<sub>m</sub>²
W<sub>lost</sub> = (I<sub>m</sub>²/2) R × T = (I<sub>m</sub>²/2) R / f₀
Q = 2π × ½LI<sub>m</sub>² / (½I<sub>m</sub>²R/f₀) = 2πf₀L/R = ω₀L/R

answer.text: Half-power frequencies. The power I²R is half its peak when I = I₀/√2, that is |Z| = R√2, so the net reactance equals ±R:
answer.pre:
ωL − 1/(ωC) = ±R
LCω² ∓ RCω − 1 = 0
ω = ±R/(2L) + √(R²/(4L²) + 1/(LC))      (positive root)
ω₁,₂ = ω₀(√(1 + 1/(4Q²)) ∓ 1/(2Q))      using R/(2L) = ω₀/(2Q)

ω₂ − ω₁ = R/L = ω₀/Q            →  BW = f₂ − f₁ = f₀/Q = R/(2πL)
ω₁ω₂ = ω₀²[(1 + 1/(4Q²)) − 1/(4Q²)] = ω₀²   →  f₀ = √(f₁f₂)

answer: So f₀ is the geometric mean of the half-power frequencies, not their average; the average is f₀√(1 + 1/(4Q²)), which is within 0.2 % of f₀ for Q ≥ 10.

answer.text: Effect of varying Q. Keep L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF (f₀ = 1591.5 Hz) and change R:

answer: Reading the table: f₀ never moves; a higher Q gives a narrower band and better selectivity; at low Q the band is visibly lopsided (1591.5 − 1304.8 = 287 Hz below, 1941.4 − 1591.5 = 350 Hz above). With a fixed source the peak current V/R also rises as R falls, and V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>C</sub> = QV grows, which is why a high-Q circuit can produce dangerous capacitor voltages.

bank.q: Define self-inductance, mutual inductance and the coefficient of coupling. Derive M = k√(L₁L₂) and explain why k cannot exceed 1.
outline: M² = k₁k₂L₁L₂, so M = k√(L₁L₂) with k = √(k₁k₂)
answer: Self-inductance. A current i in a coil of N turns sets up flux Φ per turn. L = NΦ/i, the flux linkage per ampere, in henry. A changing current induces e = −L di/dt in the same coil, opposing the change (Lenz's law).

Mutual inductance. If coil 1 carries i₁ and a part Φ₂₁ of its flux links the N₂ turns of coil 2, M = N₂Φ₂₁/i₁, and a changing i₁ induces e₂ = −M di₁/dt in coil 2. For linear media the same M results when coil 2 drives coil 1: M = N₁Φ₁₂/i₂.

answer.text: Derivation. Let a fraction k₁ of coil 1's flux link coil 2, and k₂ of coil 2's flux link coil 1:
answer.pre:
Φ₂₁ = k₁Φ₁,  Φ₁₂ = k₂Φ₂
M = N₂k₁Φ₁/i₁   and   M = N₁k₂Φ₂/i₂
M² = k₁k₂ (N₁Φ₁/i₁)(N₂Φ₂/i₂) = k₁k₂ L₁L₂
M = k√(L₁L₂),   k = √(k₁k₂)

answer: Coefficient of coupling. k = M/√(L₁L₂) is the fraction of flux shared, with no unit. Iron-core transformers reach k close to 1; separated air-core coils may have k of 0.1 or less.

answer.text: Why k ≤ 1. Each k₁, k₂ is a fraction of a flux, so neither exceeds 1, and so neither does √(k₁k₂). The energy view gives the same bound:
answer.pre:
W = ½L₁i₁² + ½L₂i₂² − M i₁i₂     (the worst sign)
put i₂ = (M/L₂) i₁:   W = ½ i₁² (L₁ − M²/L₂)
W ≥ 0 for every current  →  M² ≤ L₁L₂  →  k ≤ 1

answer: Check with numbers. L₁ = 4 H, L₂ = 1 H, k = 0.5: M = 0.5 × √4 = 1 H, below √(L₁L₂) = 2 H. With di₁/dt = 2 A/s, |e₁| = 8 V and |e₂| = 2 V.

bank.q: What is a locus diagram? Derive and sketch the current locus of a series RL circuit (i) when R is varied with X<sub>L</sub> fixed and (ii) when X<sub>L</sub> is varied with R fixed. Show where the power is maximum.
outline: Locus: path of a phasor tip as one parameter varies, V fixed as reference
R varied: |I| = (V/X<sub>L</sub>) sin θ, circle of diameter V/X<sub>L</sub> on the −90° axis
X<sub>L</sub> varied: |I| = (V/R) cos θ, circle of diameter V/R on the V axis
Only the lagging half is used
Maximum power at R = X<sub>L</sub> (45°), P = V²/(2X<sub>L</sub>)
answer: Locus diagram. The path traced by the tip of a phasor, here the current, when one element or the frequency changes while the supply voltage stays fixed. Take V as the reference phasor along the horizontal axis; lagging currents are drawn below it.

answer.text: (i) R varied, XL fixed. Let θ be the angle by which I lags V:
answer.pre:
I = V/(R + jX<sub>L</sub>),   tan θ = X<sub>L</sub>/R
|I| = V/√(R² + X<sub>L</sub>²)
sin θ = X<sub>L</sub>/√(R² + X<sub>L</sub>²)
|I| = (V/X<sub>L</sub>) sin θ

answer: In polar form r = D sin θ is a circle through the origin with diameter D = V/X<sub>L</sub> lying along the −90° axis. R = 0 gives θ = 90° and I = V/X<sub>L</sub> at the bottom of the circle; R → ∞ gives θ → 0 and I → 0. Only R ≥ 0 is real, so the locus is the right-hand semicircle.

answer.pre:
cos θ = R/√(R² + X<sub>L</sub>²)
|I| = (V/R) cos θ

answer: r = D cos θ is a circle through the origin with diameter D = V/R along the V axis. X<sub>L</sub> = 0 gives I = V/R in phase with V; X<sub>L</sub> → ∞ gives I → 0 at −90°. The locus is the lower semicircle.

Left: with reactance 10 ohms and resistance varied, a semicircle of diameter 10 amps below the voltage axis, on the minus 90 degree axis. Right: with resistance 10 ohms and reactance varied, a semicircle of diameter 10 amps along the voltage axis, below it. Both pass through 7.07 amps at minus 45 degrees, the maximum power point.

answer: Maximum power. P = VI cos θ is V times the horizontal coordinate of the tip. In (i) the right-most point of the semicircle is at θ = 45°, where R = XL, I = V/(XL√2) and Pmax = V²/(2XL). In (ii) the horizontal coordinate is largest at XL = 0, P = V²/R.

answer.text: Check with numbers for (i). V = 100 V, XL = 10 Ω, diameter 10 A, centre at 5 A below the origin:

answer: Every point is 5 A from the centre, so all lie on the semicircle, and the largest power, 500 W = 100²/(2 × 10), is at R = 10 Ω.

bank.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 100 mH and C = 10 μF and is fed from a 20 V variable-frequency source. Find f₀, Q, the bandwidth, the exact and approximate half-power frequencies, the current at resonance and the voltage across the capacitor at resonance.
outline: Exact f₁ = 151.40 Hz, f₂ = 167.31 Hz; approximate 151.20 and 167.11 Hz
answer: Data: R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H, C = 10 × 10⁻⁶ F, V = 20 V rms.
Current at resonance. Z = R, so I₀ = V/R = 20/10 = 2 A rms, in phase with V. The power is I₀²R = 40 W; at f₁ and f₂ it is 20 W.

answer.pre:
V<sub>C</sub> = I₀ X<sub>C</sub> = 2 × 100 = 200 V = QV
V<sub>L</sub> = I₀ X<sub>L</sub> = 200 V, 180° from V<sub>C</sub>

answer: Checks. f₂ − f₁ = 167.31 − 151.40 = 15.91 Hz ≈ BW. √(151.40 × 167.31) = 159.16 Hz ≈ f₀. The capacitor must be rated for 200 V although the source is only 20 V: voltage magnification by Q = 10.

bank.q: A coil of inductance 200 mH and resistance 20 Ω is connected in parallel with a 5 μF capacitor across a 230 V variable-frequency supply. Find the resonant frequency, the dynamic resistance, the supply current, the coil current and the capacitor current at resonance.
answer: Data: L = 0.2 H, r = 20 Ω, C = 5 × 10⁻⁶ F, V = 230 V. The coil resistance is not negligible, so use the practical-tank formula.
Supply current. Is = V/RD = 230/2000 = 0.115 A, in phase with V (unity power factor).

answer.pre: I<sub>C</sub> = V ω₀ C = 230 × 994.99 × 5 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.144 A, leading V by 90°

answer: The reactive parts cancel and only 0.115 A comes from the supply while 1.15 A circulates: current magnification Q = ω₀L/r = 9.95. Also r(1 + Q²) = 20 × 100 = 2000 Ω = R<sub>D</sub>.

bank.q: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Find the cutoff frequency, the gain in dB and the phase at 100 Hz, 1 kHz, f<sub>c</sub> and 10 kHz, and sketch the magnitude and phase response.
outline: Sketch on a log axis: flat, −3 dB at f<sub>c</sub>, then −20 dB per decade; phase 0 to −90°

answer.text: Transfer function. Output across C, input across R and C in series:
answer.pre:
H(jω) = (1/(jωC)) / (R + 1/(jωC)) = 1/(1 + jωRC) = 1/(1 + j f/f<sub>c</sub>)
|H| = 1/√(1 + (f/f<sub>c</sub>)²),   φ = −arctan(f/f<sub>c</sub>),   gain in dB = 20 log₁₀|H|

answer: Magnitude sketch. On a log frequency axis the gain is flat at 0 dB well below fc, passes −3 dB at 1591.5 Hz, and above it falls on a straight line of −20 dB per decade (asymptote: −20 log₁₀(f/fc), which gives −16.0 dB at 10 kHz against the true −16.07 dB).
Phase sketch. The phase starts near 0°, is −45° at fc, and tends to −90° at high frequency; it moves fastest around fc, from about −6° at fc/10 to −84° at 10 fc.
Check. At fc the two terms in 1 + jωRC are equal, so |H| = 1/√2 and φ = −45°: half power, as the table shows. The output always lags the input, as it must for a low-pass.

bank.q: Two coils with L₁ = 0.4 H and L₂ = 0.9 H are connected in series. The series-aiding inductance is 1.6 H and the series-opposing inductance is 1.0 H. Find M and the coefficient of coupling k, and the equivalent inductance when the same coils are connected in parallel, aiding and opposing.
outline: L<sub>aid</sub> = L₁ + L₂ + 2M, L<sub>opp</sub> = L₁ + L₂ − 2M
Parallel: (L₁L₂ − M²)/(L₁ + L₂ ∓ 2M) = 0.3375 H and 0.2109 H

answer.text: Series equations. With one current through both coils:
answer.pre:
aiding:   L<sub>A</sub> = L₁ + L₂ + 2M = 1.6 H
opposing: L<sub>O</sub> = L₁ + L₂ − 2M = 1.0 H
L<sub>A</sub> + L<sub>O</sub> = 2(L₁ + L₂) = 2.6 H  →  L₁ + L₂ = 1.3 H = 0.4 + 0.9  ✓

answer: This is the standard test method: measure the series inductance both ways and M = (L<sub>A</sub> − L<sub>O</sub>)/4, with no need to know L₁ and L₂ separately.

answer.text: Parallel connection. Both coils share v. Aiding: v = L₁ di₁/dt + M di₂/dt = M di₁/dt + L₂ di₂/dt. Solving for the total current gives:

answer: Checks. k = 0.25 lies between 0 and 1. With no coupling the parallel value would be L₁L₂/(L₁ + L₂) = 0.36/1.3 = 0.277 H; aiding raises it and opposing lowers it, as expected.

bank.q: An ideal transformer with 500 primary turns and 100 secondary turns feeds a 4 Ω load from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the secondary voltage, the secondary current, the primary current and the impedance seen at the primary, and check the power balance.
answer: Assumptions. Ideal transformer: no winding resistance, no core loss, infinite permeability and k = 1, so the turns ratio sets every ratio exactly. Both dots on the same side, so V₂ is in phase with V₁.

answer.pre:
Z<sub>in</sub> = V₁/I₁ = 230/2.3 = 100 Ω
check: Z<sub>L</sub>/n² = 4/0.04 = 100 Ω

answer: Comment. The 50 Hz figure plays no part in an ideal transformer; it matters only for a real core (flux and magnetizing current). The transformer makes a 4 Ω load look like 100 Ω to the supply, 25 times larger: impedance scales by the square of the turns ratio, here (500/100)² = 25.

bank.q: An iron ring of mean length 50 cm and cross-section 4 cm² carries a coil of 400 turns. The relative permeability of the iron is 1500 and the ring has a 1 mm air gap. For a flux of 0.5 mWb, find the reluctance of the iron, the reluctance of the gap, the MMF and the coil current, and the inductance of the coil. Ignore fringing and leakage.
outline: Check with H drops; L = N²/R<sub>total</sub> = 60 mH
answer: Data: l<sub>i</sub> = 0.5 m (the 1 mm gap is neglected in the iron length), A = 4 × 10⁻⁴ m², μ<sub>r</sub> = 1500, l<sub>g</sub> = 10⁻³ m, N = 400, Φ = 0.5 × 10⁻³ Wb, μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.

answer.text: Total reluctance, MMF and current. The same flux passes through iron and gap, so the reluctances are in series:
Check by MMF drops. B = Φ/A = 0.5×10⁻³/4×10⁻⁴ = 1.25 T in both parts:

answer: The 1 mm gap takes 75 % of the MMF although it is 1/500 of the path length, because its permeability is 1500 times lower.
Comment. B = 1.25 T is near the knee of many steels, so in practice μr would be checked on the B-H curve; the question fixes μr = 1500, so the answer stands: I ≈ 3.32 A.

bank.q: A coil of resistance 4 Ω and variable inductance is connected in parallel with a capacitor of reactance 10 Ω across a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. Using the locus of the coil current, find the values of inductance that make the circuit resonant and the supply current in each case.
outline: Coil current locus: semicircle of diameter V/R = 50 A below V
Add I<sub>C</sub> = 20 A at +90°: the circle shifts up
Resonance where the shifted circle cuts the V axis
X<sub>L</sub>² − X<sub>C</sub> X<sub>L</sub> + R² = 0 → X<sub>L</sub> = 8 Ω or 2 Ω
L = 25.5 mH or 6.37 mH; I = 10 A or 40 A

answer.text: Locus of the coil current. With R = 4 Ω fixed and XL varied, the coil current runs on a circle of diameter V/R along the V axis:
answer.pre: diameter = 200/4 = 50 A, centre (25, 0) A, radius 25 A, lower (lagging) half

answer: Capacitor current. IC = V/XC = 200/10 = 20 A, leading V by 90°. It is the same for every XL, so the total-current locus is the coil semicircle shifted 20 A upward: the centre of the circle moves from (25, 0) to (25, 20) A. Its lower half now runs from (50, 20) at XL = 0, down below the V axis, and back up toward (0, 20) as XL grows.

answer.text: Where it cuts the V axis. The shifted circle is (x − 25)² + (y − 20)² = 25². At y = 0:

answer: So the supply current is in phase with V (resonance) at 10 A and at 40 A. Two points exist because the shift, 20 A, is less than the radius, 25 A; that is the same as X<sub>C</sub> > 2R (10 Ω > 8 Ω).

answer.text: The matching inductances (algebra). Susceptances cancel when XL/(R² + XL²) = 1/XC:

answer: Check. The admittance at resonance is R/(R² + XL²): 4/80 = 0.05 S gives 200 × 0.05 = 10 A, and 4/20 = 0.2 S gives 40 A, matching the locus. The larger inductance, 25.5 mH, gives the smaller supply current and the higher dynamic resistance (20 Ω against 5 Ω).

bank.q: Compare series and parallel resonance in detail: impedance and current at resonance, the role of R, the meaning of Q, magnification, and the effect of Q on bandwidth and selectivity. Use one numerical pair of circuits and a radio tuner as the application.
outline: Series: Z = R minimum, current maximum, acceptor, voltage magnification
Parallel: Z maximum, supply current minimum, rejector, current magnification
Q: ω₀L/R series, R/(ω₀L) parallel; R plays opposite roles
Tuner: high Q selects one channel; practical limits
answer: Common ground. Both circuits resonate when the reactive effects of L and C cancel. For ideal elements both give ω₀ = 1/√(LC), and in both the bandwidth between half-power points is f₀/Q.

head: Property
Series RLC
Parallel RLC (ideal tank)
rows: maximum, Z = R (R<sub>D</sub> = L/(rC) for a real coil)

answer: Why R plays opposite roles. In series, R carries the full current and dissipates I²R; a larger R wastes more energy per cycle, so Q falls. In parallel, R carries V/R; a larger R draws less current and wastes less, so Q rises. Q = 2π × stored/lost per cycle in both.

answer.text: One numerical pair. L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF in both, 10 V source; series R = 10 Ω, parallel R = 1 kΩ:

answer: The two circuits have the same f₀, Q and bandwidth, yet the series one draws 100 times more current: it is the low-impedance dual of the parallel one.

answer.text: Effect of Q on selectivity. For the series band-pass |H| = 1/√(1 + Q²(f/f₀ − f₀/f)²). At f = 1.1 f₀:

answer: So a five-times higher Q rejects a signal 10 % off tune about 4.5 times more strongly in amplitude: higher Q means a narrower band and sharper selectivity.

Radio tuner. An AM receiver stage uses a parallel LC tank as the load of an amplifier: its high impedance at f₀ gives high gain for the wanted station and low gain for others. Tuning a variable capacitor moves f₀. The required Q is f₀/BW: for a 10 kHz channel at 1 MHz, Q = 100. A series LC (acceptor) is used where a low-impedance path to one frequency is wanted, such as a trap that shorts an unwanted signal to ground.
Limits. Too high a Q cuts the edges of the wanted channel and makes tuning sensitive to drift; coil resistance and loading by the amplifier set the highest Q that can be reached.
Check. VC = QV = 10 × 10 = 100 V in the series circuit and IC = Q × 10 mA = 100 mA in the parallel one; both agree with the table.

bank.q: A 50∠0° V source with R₁ = 4 Ω drives a coil of reactance 8 Ω. It is coupled (ωM = 6 Ω) to a coil of reactance 12 Ω that feeds a 6 Ω load. Mesh current I₁ enters the dot of coil 1 and I₂ leaves the dot of coil 2. Write the mesh equations, find I₁, I₂ and the load power, express the result as a reflected impedance, and explain what changes if one dot is reversed.
outline: Dot rule: one current enters, one leaves → −jωM terms
Reversed dot: sign of M flips, I₁ unchanged, I₂ reversed
answer: Signs from the dots. I₁ enters the dotted terminal of coil 1 and I₂ leaves the dotted terminal of coil 2. One current enters a dot and the other leaves one, so the fluxes oppose and each mutual term is −jωM = −j6 Ω.

answer.pre:
Mesh 1:  (4 + j8) I₁ − j6 I₂ = 50
Mesh 2:  −j6 I₁ + (6 + j12) I₂ = 0

answer.text: Solve for I₁ through the reflected impedance. From mesh 2, I₂ = j6 I₁/(6 + j12). Substituting:

answer: The real part of the reflected impedance, 1.2 Ω, carries exactly the load power: the primary sees the load through the coupling. Its imaginary part, −j2.4 Ω, is negative because the secondary is inductive; coupling an inductive secondary lowers the primary's apparent inductance.

One dot reversed. Now both currents enter (or both leave) dotted terminals, so the mutual terms become +j6. Mesh 2 gives I₂ = −j6 I₁/(6 + j12), and substituting into mesh 1 gives j6 × (−j6)/(6 + j12) = +36/(6 + j12) again: the reflected impedance depends on (ωM)², so the sign of M drops out. Zin and I₁ do not change; I₂ changes sign, I₂ = 2.926∠159.4° A, and the load power stays 51.4 W.

What this means. A dot error never changes the power or the current magnitudes in a two-winding circuit, but it reverses the phase of the secondary. It matters when windings are connected together (series aiding against opposing) or paralleled, where a reversed dot changes the result completely.
Coupling check. k = ωM/√(ωL₁ × ωL₂) = 6/√(8 × 12) = 0.61, below 1, so the data are physical.

bank.q: A receiver front-end tuned to 1 MHz must pass a 10 kHz wide channel and reject a station 20 kHz away. Using the series band-pass response, compare Q = 50, 100 and 200 and recommend a Q. Discuss what limits the highest usable Q in practice.
outline: Q = f₀/BW = 100 for a 10 kHz band
|H| = 1/√(1 + Q²(f/f₀ − f₀/f)²) at ±5 kHz and +20 kHz
Choose about 100; limits: coil r, loading, drift
answer: Requirement. The channel spans 995 kHz to 1005 kHz. A half-power bandwidth of 10 kHz needs Q = f₀/BW = 1 000 000/10 000 = 100.

answer.text: Response used. For the series RLC band-pass:

head: Q
BW (kHz)
Gain at channel edge
Gain at +20 kHz
Verdict
rows: best rejection, cuts the channel edges

answer: Sample working for Q = 100 at the neighbour: Q(x − 1/x) = 3.961; |H| = 1/√(1 + 15.69) = 1/4.085 = 0.245; 20 log₁₀ 0.245 = −12.2 dB.

Judgement. Q = 50 passes the whole channel but lets the neighbour through at nearly half amplitude. Q = 200 rejects the neighbour well but attenuates the channel edges by 7 dB, which distorts the audio (high audio frequencies sit at the edges). Q = 100 is the balanced choice: the edges are at exactly the half-power level and the neighbour is down 12 dB. More rejection is better obtained with two tuned stages of Q ≈ 100 (−24 dB at the neighbour) than with one stage of Q = 200.

head: Limit
Effect
rows: For L = 100 µH at 1 MHz, ω₀L = 628 Ω; Q = 100 needs r ≤ 6.3 Ω including skin effect
The source and the next stage add resistance and lower the loaded Q
A 1 % change in C moves f₀ by 0.5 % = 5 kHz, half the band at Q = 100
A steep phase change near f₀ delays the band edges differently and distorts the signal

answer: Check. At Q = 100 the edge gain 0.708 ≈ 1/√2, as the definition of bandwidth requires, which confirms the table.

bank.q: A three-limb core carries a 400-turn coil on the centre limb (length 0.15 m, area 6 cm²). Each outer limb is 0.35 m long with area 3 cm². μ<sub>r</sub> = 800 throughout. Draw the magnetic equivalent circuit and find the coil current needed for a flux of 0.3 mWb in each outer limb. Check your answer by the MMF round one loop.
outline: Equivalent circuit: MMF source and centre reluctance in series with the two outer reluctances in parallel
answer: Equivalent circuit. The coil on the centre limb is the MMF source F = NI. The centre limb is a reluctance Rc in series with the source. At the top and bottom yokes the flux splits into the two outer limbs, Ro each, which are in parallel with each other. Yoke lengths are included in the outer-limb lengths given.

answer.text: Flux and MMF. By symmetry the centre flux is the sum of the two outer fluxes:
answer.pre:
Φ<sub>c</sub> = 2 × 0.3 = 0.6 mWb
R<sub>total</sub> = R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>o</sub>/2 = 2.49×10⁵ + 5.80×10⁵ = 8.29×10⁵ A/Wb
F = Φ<sub>c</sub> R<sub>total</sub> = 0.6×10⁻³ × 8.29×10⁵ = 497 A
I = F/N = 497/400 = 1.24 A

answer.text: Check round one loop (centre limb plus one outer limb):

answer: The equal flux density is why the outer limbs are given half the centre area in a shell-type core: the iron is used evenly.

If the core were not symmetric (different outer limbs), the fluxes would split in inverse ratio of the outer reluctances, Φ₁/Φ₂ = R₂/R₁, because the same MMF drop appears across both outer limbs. The method is unchanged: combine the parallel limbs, find the total flux, then split it.
Comment. μr is taken as constant. At 1.0 T most electrical steels are below the knee, so the linear model is reasonable here.

glossary.def: The condition in a circuit containing L and C where the two reactances cancel and the circuit behaves purely resistively.
The frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) at which cancellation of reactances occurs.
The imaginary part of impedance: X<sub>L</sub> = 2πfL for a coil and X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(2πfC) for a capacitor, both in ohm.
The imaginary part of admittance, in siemens; parallel resonance occurs when the total susceptance is zero.
A frequency where the power delivered is half the resonant value, which means the current is 1/√2 of its peak.
The difference between the two half-power frequencies, equal to f₀/Q in hertz.
A dimensionless number comparing energy stored per cycle with energy lost per cycle; higher Q means a sharper, narrower response.
How well a tuned circuit separates the wanted frequency band from unwanted nearby frequencies.
The resistance L/(rC) that a practical parallel tank presents at resonance, with r the coil resistance.
The frequency at which the gain of a first-order circuit drops to 0.707 of its maximum, a 3 dB fall.
A tenfold change in frequency; first-order filters change gain by 20 dB per decade beyond cutoff.
The property of a coil that opposes change of its own current by inducing a voltage proportional to di/dt.
The property by which a changing current in one coil induces a voltage in a second coil linked by common flux.
The product NΦ, the total flux threading all turns of a coil, measured in weber-turns.
k = M/√(L₁L₂), the measure of how much flux two coils share; it lies between 0 and 1.
A pair of marks on coupled coils such that currents entering both dots create flux in the same direction.
A connection where the two coupled coils carry current into the dotted terminals, giving L<sub>eq</sub> = L₁ + L₂ + 2M.
A connection where one coil is reversed so its flux opposes the other, giving L<sub>eq</sub> = L₁ + L₂ − 2M.
A lossless transformer with infinite magnetizing inductance and unity coupling, giving exact turns-ratio scaling of voltage and current.
A coupled-coil model with finite self and mutual inductances, analysed by mesh equations; it is linear but not ideal.
The driving force of a magnetic circuit, MMF = NI, measured in ampere-turns.
The opposition a magnetic path offers to flux, R = l/(μA), in ampere-turns per weber.
The property μ = μ₀μ<sub>r</sub> of a material showing how easily it carries magnetic flux, in henry per metre.
A short non-magnetic length in a magnetic core; its reluctance is high, so it often takes most of the MMF and stores most of the energy.
The path traced by the tip of a phasor when one circuit element or the frequency varies and the supply voltage is fixed.
The impedance (ωM)²/(jωL₂ + Z<sub>L</sub>) that a loaded secondary adds to the primary of a linear transformer.
The angle of H(jω) against frequency: how far the output leads or lags the input.
A parallel resonant tank, so called because it draws minimum current from the supply at f₀.
